title: Proximity Service (Yelp-style 'Nearby')
problem: Design a proximity / 'find businesses near me' service like Yelp, Google Maps nearby, or DoorDash restaurant search.
summary: A read-heavy geospatial lookup service that must answer 'all restaurants within R meters of (lat, lng)' in under ~100ms p99. The dominant design choice is a pre-computed geohash (or quadtree) index: every business is tagged with its geohash cell, and a radius query becomes 'fetch businesses in this cell + 8 neighbor cells'. A Redis layer caches hot cells (Times Square, downtown SF) which absorb the vast majority of queries; PostGIS on Postgres is the authoritative store with GiST indexes for exact radius filtering. The main tradeoff is precision vs cacheability: coarse geohash cells (6 chars ≈ 1.2 km) cache beautifully but include far-away businesses that need post-filtering; fine cells (8 chars ≈ 38 m) need 8+ cell fetches per query. Sized for 500M DAU with ~5B nearby-search QPS/year.

functional: Register, update, and delete business listings with (lat, lng, category, hours, metadata).
Return all businesses within radius R meters of a user coordinate, ranked by distance.
Support category filters (restaurant, pharmacy, ATM) and optional open-now filter.
Paginate with a stable cursor so map panning does not re-render duplicates.
Admin-only bulk import pipeline for partner data feeds (Yelp Fusion, OSM).
Expose a /businesses/{id} detail endpoint for the map pin popover.
nonFunctional: p99 read latency under 100 ms for radius <= 5 km at 35K peak QPS.
85% or higher Redis cell cache hit ratio on the hot 1000 cells.
Eventual consistency of 60 s is acceptable for listing edits; reads are not transactional.
Regional isolation: a Tokyo region outage must not affect San Francisco traffic.
Cost per million reads under $0.20 amortised across cache plus PostGIS.
Horizontally scalable by adding PostGIS shards keyed on geohash prefix.

assumptions: Hot cell distribution: top 1000 geohash cells (cities + landmarks) handle ~40% of all queries
Business listings update ~1M times/day (new, closed, edited hours)
estimates: Cache working set: 1000 hot cells * avg 100 KB payload ≈ 100 MB — trivially fits a single Redis node, replicated for HA
PostGIS size: 200M rows * avg 1 KB = 200 GB + GiST index ≈ 250 GB — fits on a modest sharded Postgres
Update QPS: 1M / 86400 ≈ 12 QPS peak — write path is not the bottleneck
Cache hit ratio target: 85%+ on hot cells → only ~1.7K QPS reach PostGIS at steady state

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> api[Proximity API] api --> loc[Location Service] api --> geoidx[(Geohash Index)] api --> cache[(Redis Cell Cache)] api --> pg[(Businesses DB)] api --> userloc[User-Location Service]

client.name: Client (Mobile App / Web)
client.summary: Mobile app or web page that asks the OS for (lat, lng) and calls /nearby with a radius.

sections.heading: Location
sections.body: Uses the OS geolocation API (CoreLocation / FusedLocationProvider / navigator.geolocation). Accuracy 5–30 m outdoors, 50–500 m indoors.

sections.heading: Request shape
sections.body:
```
GET /nearby?lat=37.7749&lng=-122.4194&radius=500&category=restaurant&limit=20
```
Radius is capped server-side to 50 km to keep queries bounded.

sections.heading: Rendering
sections.body: Renders results on a map; prefetches next-page results as the user pans. Uses a local in-memory dedupe by business_id so a panning map doesn't re-render duplicates.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client picks the radius. A user zoomed out to 'the whole city' triggers an entirely different query shape than 'next block over' — the backend must handle both with the same cheap index.

bottlenecks.title: OS geolocation cold-fix latency dominates p99
bottlenecks.trigger: First /nearby call after app launch or after moving indoors — CoreLocation/FusedLocationProvider can take 2–30s for a GPS fix, and indoor accuracy degrades to 50–500m vs the 5–30m outdoor baseline.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sees a spinner long before any HTTP request is made; when results do load they are for the wrong block (stale/low-accuracy fix), causing 'why is this showing restaurants a mile away?' complaints.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Request location with a timeout (e.g. getCurrentPosition maximumAge=60000, timeout=3000) and fall back to the last cached fix or coarse IP-geolocation; show results immediately and re-issue /nearby when a better fix arrives. Warm the location provider on app foreground before the user taps search.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry histogram of time-to-first-fix and accuracy_m per /nearby call; alert when p95 time-to-fix > 2s or p50 accuracy > 100m for >5% of sessions.

bottlenecks.title: Map panning causes /nearby request storms
bottlenecks.trigger: User pans/zooms the map continuously; each viewport change can fire a /nearby call. At 500M DAU with 2 searches/user/day baseline, a 10x panning multiplier on even 5% of sessions pushes peak QPS from 35K toward 150K+, well beyond the 15-replica API fleet sizing.
bottlenecks.symptom: Backend sees bursty traffic spikes, Redis cell cache hit ratio drops below the 85% target as unusual cells get queried, and the user perceives jank as older in-flight responses render over newer ones.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Debounce viewport-change queries (e.g. 300ms trailing), cancel in-flight fetches with AbortController on new pans, and snap the query center to the current geohash-6 cell so small pans reuse the same cached response. Maintain the local in-memory dedupe by business_id already described.
bottlenecks.detection: Client metric 'nearby_requests_per_session_minute' and server-side ratio of /nearby QPS to DAU; alert when per-session request rate exceeds 10/min p95 or when cache hit ratio dips below 80%.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded radius / limit abuse from the client
bottlenecks.trigger: A zoomed-out 'whole city' view submits radius=50km (the server cap) with limit=20, which maps to geohash precision 5 (~4.9km cells) and scans 9 large cells — payloads can be 100KB+ and candidate sets thousands of rows before the 20-row truncation.
bottlenecks.symptom: Slow responses on mobile networks, high egress bandwidth, and rendering stalls as the client parses large JSON only to drop most of it; p99 latency blows past the 100ms budget for these queries.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side clamp radius based on current map zoom level (e.g. radius = min(viewport_diagonal/2, 5km) for normal browsing); request only the fields needed for pin rendering via a?fields=id,lat,lng,name projection; paginate with the provided cursor instead of raising limit.
bottlenecks.detection: Log radius and response_size_bytes per request; alert when p95 request radius > 10km or p95 response size > 50KB, and track ratio of requested_limit vs rendered_markers to spot over-fetching.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client matters in a proximity service For a "find businesses near me" service, the client isn't just a dumb rendering surface — it's the component that *produces the query coordinates in the first place*. Unlike a URL shortener where the browser just sends a known ID, here the client has to ask the phone's OS for a GPS fix, decide the search radius based on map zoom, and frame the request shape (`lat`, `lng`, `radius`, `category`). Every downstream optimization — geohash precision selection, Redis cell caching, PostGIS pruning — is driven by numbers the client chose. Garbage in, garbage out. ## What happens without a smart client If the client naively fires a fresh `/nearby` call on every pixel of map panning, or submits `radius=50km` when the user is looking at one city block, the backend gets crushed. The user sees a spinner because GPS took 8 seconds to return a fix (and the app didn't fall back to the last known location). Operators see Redis hit ratio collapse below the 85% target because panning generates unusual, one-off geohash cells that never get reused, and PostGIS QPS spikes as those misses fall through. ## The numbers The design sizes for 1B searches/day ≈ 11.5K QPS, peak 35K. But the prebuild notes that a 10× panning multiplier on just 5% of sessions would push peak toward 150K QPS — more than 4× the provisioned fleet of ~15 API replicas. Client-side debouncing (300ms) and snapping to the current geohash-6 cell is what keeps that multiplier near 1×. ## The trade-off Pushing logic (radius clamping, debouncing, dedupe) into the client means shipping it across iOS, Android, and web — three codebases to keep in sync — in exchange for a backend that can actually meet the 100ms p99 budget.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer distributing /nearby and /businesses traffic to stateless API replicas.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin with least-connections fallback. Health check on /healthz every 2s; eject after 3 consecutive 5xx in 10s.

sections.heading: Geo routing
sections.body: If deployed multi-region, DNS-level GeoIP routes to the nearest region's LB. Each region has its own PostGIS + Redis; businesses are globally replicated but queries stay local.

gained: gRPC support for mobile native clients

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU ceiling at 35K peak QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 35K QPS of /nearby requests all arriving over HTTPS from mobile clients. Each new TLS handshake (ECDHE + cert verify) costs ~1–3ms of CPU; if mobile session resumption tickets aren't honored (app backgrounding, IP changes on cellular→wifi), a meaningful fraction become full handshakes.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU saturates before backend replicas do; connection establishment latency climbs from <5ms to 50–200ms, adding directly to the 100ms p99 budget. On-call sees LB node CPU at 90%+ while api replicas sit at 40%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT session resumption, tune session ticket lifetime to 24h, offload to hardware/AES-NI-enabled instances, and horizontally scale the LB tier (add nodes behind anycast VIP). Set keepalive_timeout=75s so mobile apps reuse connections across panning bursts instead of re-handshaking.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 70%, TLS handshake rate > 30% of request rate (indicates poor session reuse), and tls_handshake_duration_ms p95 > 20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Health-check eviction storm during PostGIS slowdowns
bottlenecks.trigger: A PostGIS replica slowdown or Redis cache flush causes API replicas to respond with 5xx or slow on /healthz. The 2s interval + 3-consecutive-5xx-in-10s policy can evict most of the 15-replica fleet within 10–15s if the failure is correlated (e.g., all replicas share the same Postgres primary).
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden drop in healthy upstream count from 15 → 3, surviving replicas instantly hit 100% CPU as 35K QPS concentrate on them, cascading more evictions. Users see a hard outage rather than degradation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple /healthz from downstream dependencies (return 200 if the process is alive; use /readyz with dependency checks only for rolling deploys). Set a minimum-healthy-hosts floor (e.g., never evict below 50% of fleet) and add outlier-detection backoff rather than binary eviction. Use panic threshold (Envoy-style: if <50% healthy, route to all).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on healthy_upstream_count dropping >30% in <30s, and on ratio of 5xx_from_upstream vs 5xx_from_lb. Track health-check failure correlation across replicas.

bottlenecks.title: GeoIP DNS routing misdirects roaming users to wrong region
bottlenecks.trigger: In multi-region deployment, a user traveling (e.g., US resident in EU) hits the EU region's LB via GeoIP DNS. The EU PostGIS shard holds EU businesses, but the user's lat/lng is in the US — or worse, carrier-grade NAT / VPN makes GeoIP wrong for a chunk of traffic (estimated 2–5% of mobile users).
bottlenecks.symptom: Users get empty /nearby results or cross-region PostGIS scatter-queries with 100–200ms cross-Atlantic latency, blowing the 100ms p99 SLO. Support tickets: 'the app shows no restaurants near me'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route by request-body lat/lng at the L7 LB (Envoy with a Lua/WASM filter extracting query params) rather than by client IP; or have each region's LB detect out-of-region coordinates and internally proxy to the correct region over a warm backhaul. Keep a global fallback cluster for ambiguous requests.
bottlenecks.detection: Log region_served vs geohash_prefix_region per request; alert when mismatch rate > 1%, and track cross-region backhaul latency p95.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a load balancer in front of the Proximity Service For a "find businesses near me" service sized at 500M DAU and ~35K peak QPS, no single API server can handle the traffic — not even close. A beefy API node might do 2–3K QPS of geohash math + Redis lookups before CPU saturates. So the design runs ~15 stateless API replicas in parallel, and *something* has to sit in front of them to spread incoming `/nearby` calls across the fleet. That's the load balancer's core job here: turn one public endpoint (`api.yelp-clone.com`) into a pool that clients don't need to know about. But it's doing more than fan-out. It terminates TLS (mobile apps all speak HTTPS), health-checks replicas every 2s so a crashed API node gets pulled from rotation before users notice, and — critically for a geospatial service — it does GeoIP-based DNS routing so a user in Paris hits the EU region's PostGIS+Redis stack, not one across the Atlantic. Without that, every query eats 100ms of transoceanic RTT and blows the 100ms p99 budget on network alone. ## What breaks without it Point the mobile app directly at one API node and you get two failure modes: that node saturates around 2–3K QPS and starts 503-ing (users see "no restaurants found"), and when it crashes, the app has no way to fail over — the whole region goes dark until someone updates DNS. ## The arithmetic 35K peak QPS ÷ ~15 API replicas ≈ 2.3K QPS per replica, comfortably under saturation. Remove the LB and you'd need clients to pick a replica themselves, which they can't do safely. ## The trade-off The LB is now a critical shared dependency — if its TLS CPU saturates or health checks misfire, it can take down the whole fleet even when the API replicas are healthy.

api.name: Proximity API
api.summary: Stateless service that owns /nearby, /businesses CRUD, and orchestrates the cache→index→DB lookup chain.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
GET /nearby?lat=&lng=&radius=&category=&limit=
GET /businesses/:id
POST /businesses # new listing (owner)
PATCH /businesses/:id # edit hours, category, etc.
```

sections.heading: Nearby query algorithm
sections.body:
1. Compute geohash of (lat, lng) at precision P (derived from radius)
2. Compute 8 neighbor cells (covers edge cases at cell boundaries)
3. For each of 9 cells: try Redis cache
4. Cache misses fall through to PostGIS `ST_DWithin` exact query
5. Union, filter by category, sort by distance, truncate to limit

sections.heading: Precision mapping
sections.body:
```
radius ≤ 200m → geohash 8 (38 m)
radius ≤ 1 km → geohash 7 (150 m)
radius ≤ 5 km → geohash 6 (1.2 km)
radius ≤ 20 km → geohash 5 (4.9 km)
radius > 20 km → geohash 4 (39 km)
```
Choice: pick the coarsest cell that's ≤ the radius, to minimize number of cells to fetch.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU. Peak 35K QPS / 10ms avg → ~350 concurrent reqs/replica; run ~15 replicas for headroom.

gained: Zero fleet ops, autoscale to zero overnight
lost: Cold starts blow the 100ms p99 budget
Persistent PostGIS connection pool is awkward from Lambda

bottlenecks.title: Cache stampede on popular cell expiry
bottlenecks.trigger: A hot cell like Times Square serves ~14 QPS and its 5-min TTL expires simultaneously across all ~30 category variants. With 40% of 35K peak QPS (~14K QPS) concentrated on top-1000 cells, a synchronized expiry on a popular (cell, category) pair sends hundreds of concurrent requests per API replica through to PostGIS for the same ST_DWithin query.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 5-min latency spikes where p99 jumps from ~15ms to 200ms+, PostGIS connection pool saturates (pool size ~50/replica × 15 replicas = 750 connections vs Postgres max ~500), and the LB reports elevated 503s from timeout.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use single-flight / request coalescing in the API (e.g. groupcache-style per-key in-flight map) so only one request per (cell, category) fills the cache on miss. Add TTL jitter (±60s) to decorrelate expiry across cells, and use stale-while-revalidate: serve stale cell data up to 30s past TTL while refreshing asynchronously.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on PostGIS QPS > 3K (2× steady-state expectation of 1.7K), on api_cache_miss_ratio spikes >20% for >10s, and on p99 latency bimodal distribution. Track in-flight-dedupe counter per (cell, category).

bottlenecks.title: Wrong geohash precision inflates candidate set
bottlenecks.trigger: A 500m radius maps to precision 7 (~150m cells) requiring 9 cells, but a 2km radius maps to precision 6 (~1.2km cells) where each of 9 cells holds ~30 businesses — fine. The pathological case is radius=600m (just over the precision-7 boundary → precision 6), where 9 × 1.2km cells yield 200–500 candidates needing Haversine post-filter on every request. At 35K QPS, that's 7–17M haversine computations/sec across the fleet.
bottlenecks.symptom: CPU on API replicas climbs to 80%+ on distance math rather than I/O wait; p50 latency drifts from 8ms toward 20ms; horizontal scaling past 15 replicas shows diminishing returns because each request is CPU-bound.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adopt S2 cells or variable-precision geohash where precision is chosen to minimize cells-fetched × candidates-per-cell jointly, not just 'coarsest cell ≤ radius'. Pre-compute ST_Distance-sorted cell listings in Redis so post-filter becomes a truncation, not a sort. Vectorize haversine (SIMD / numpy-style batch) for 5–10× speedup on the 200–500 candidate case.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram of candidates_evaluated_per_request; alert when p95 > 300. Track cpu_time_ms vs wall_time_ms per request — a ratio > 0.6 indicates CPU-bound on distance math rather than I/O-bound on Redis/PG.

bottlenecks.title: Invalidation SCAN on PATCH blocks the event loop
bottlenecks.trigger: A PATCH /businesses/:id that changes location requires SCAN+DEL on `near:{cell}:*` for 9 affected cells × ~30 categories = ~270 keys, plus the Redis SCAN itself is O(N) over the full keyspace (~30K keys). At 12 writes/sec this is fine in steady state, but a bulk import or admin backfill (e.g. 10K business relocations after a map-data refresh) sends SCAN QPS to thousands/sec, blocking Redis single-threaded command execution.
bottlenecks.symptom: During bulk writes, /nearby read latency from the same Redis cluster spikes to 50–100ms as SCAN commands queue ahead of MGETs; cache hit ratio drops because SETs from backfill also contend; on-call sees Redis CPU pinned at 100%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a reverse index `cell_keys:{cell}` as a Redis SET of live category keys per cell, so invalidation becomes SMEMBERS + DEL (O(categories) ~30 ops) instead of SCAN (O(keyspace)). Rate-limit bulk-write invalidation via a queue (e.g. 100 invalidations/sec) and use UNLINK instead of DEL for non-blocking deletion.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis SCAN command rate > 10/sec, on Redis commandstats p99 latency > 5ms, and on PATCH-driven invalidation-fan-out exceeding 500 keys/sec. Track cache_key_count per cell to catch keyspace bloat.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Proximity API exists here For a Yelp-style "nearby" service, the client sends a deceptively simple request: "give me restaurants within 500m of this lat/lng." But nothing downstream speaks that language. PostGIS wants a `ST_DWithin` SQL query with a geography point. Redis wants a key like `near:9q8zn8u:restaurant`. The geohash index wants a cell string at the right precision. *Something* has to translate one HTTP call into the cache→index→DB lookup chain, pick the right geohash precision for the radius, fan out to 9 neighbor cells, merge results, post-filter by exact Haversine distance, and sort. That orchestration *is* the Proximity API. It's the only stateful decision-maker in the read path — everything else (Redis, PostGIS, Location Service) is a dumb lookup. ## What breaks without it Push this logic into the mobile client and every iOS/Android/web app needs to know your geohash scheme, your Redis keys, and your PostGIS connection string — a security nightmare and impossible to evolve. Push it into PostGIS via stored procedures and you lose the Redis cache layer entirely, sending all 35K peak QPS straight at the database, which tops out around 300 concurrent queries per node. ## The arithmetic Peak load is **35K QPS** with a ~10ms average service time per request. That means ~350 concurrent in-flight requests at any moment. A single API replica handles ~2–3K QPS comfortably, so 35K ÷ 2.3K ≈ **15 replicas** — stateless, CPU-bound, horizontally scalable. Remove the API tier and there's no place to run the "pick precision 7 for 500m radius" logic that makes the whole cache layer cacheable in the first place. ## The trade-off Adding this tier costs one extra network hop (~1–2ms) and 15 servers of operational surface area in exchange for keeping the clients dumb and the storage layer replaceable.

loc.name: Location Service
loc.summary: Thin helper service that encapsulates geohash / quadtree math and business-to-cell indexing.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: Pure computation + a tiny in-memory index of cell → business_id list, rebuilt from PostGIS on a 1-min interval. The Proximity API calls it to get the candidate set before hitting Redis or PostGIS.

sections.heading: Why split it out
sections.body:
- Keeps geohash/quadtree code (and possibly S2 cells) in one library
- Lets us swap the spatial index (geohash → quadtree → S2) without touching the API
- In-memory candidate index is small (200M business_ids * 16 B ≈ 3.2 GB) and rebuildable

sections.heading: Refresh
sections.body: Subscribes to a Postgres logical-replication stream of business inserts/updates/deletes; updates its in-memory cell → business_id multimap with <1s lag.

gained: Cells subdivide where density is high — Manhattan gets fine cells, rural gets coarse
lost: Tree pointers don't cache as flatly as geohash strings

gained: Better shape at high latitudes (no pole distortion)
Hierarchical cell IDs support range queries naturally
lost: Less human-readable than geohash (64-bit ints vs short strings)

bottlenecks.title: In-memory index rebuild blocks candidate lookups on restart
bottlenecks.trigger: Process restart (deploy, OOM, node replacement) forces a full reload of the 200M business_id → cell multimap (~3.2 GB) from PostGIS; the stated ~30s reload window coincides with 35K peak QPS of /nearby traffic, meaning ~1M requests must bypass the Location Service during bootstrap.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rolling deploys, p99 latency spikes from ~15ms to 100–300ms as the Proximity API falls back directly to PostGIS ST_DWithin scans without the candidate-id shortcut; PostGIS connection pool saturates (300 concurrency limit) and users see intermittent 503s or empty results.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Snapshot the RoaringBitmap index to disk/S3 every 5 min and mmap it on startup (reload in 2–5s instead of 30s); stagger replica restarts with a readiness gate that only flips /readyz green after the index is loaded AND replication lag is <2s; keep N+2 replicas so at most one is rebuilding at any time.
bottlenecks.detection: Gauge `loc_index_ready` (0/1) and `loc_index_load_seconds` per replica; alert when any replica reports not-ready for >10s or when the fraction of ready replicas drops below 80%. Track PostGIS fallback QPS as a leading indicator.

bottlenecks.title: Replication-stream lag causes stale candidate sets
bottlenecks.trigger: The 1M/day business updates translate to ~12 writes/sec steady state, but bulk admin imports or map-data refreshes (e.g. 10K relocations at once) can burst the Postgres logical-replication stream well past the consumer's apply rate, pushing the advertised <1s lag to tens of seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Newly relocated businesses continue to appear in their old geohash cell's candidate list and are missing from the new cell; /nearby returns phantom results (businesses outside the actual radius that pass the candidate filter but fail Haversine post-filter) or misses newly-added hot spots for minutes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parallelize the replication consumer by sharding on business_id hash (e.g. 8 workers) so throughput scales past single-threaded apply; add backpressure by pausing bulk-import tools when `loc_replication_lag_seconds > 5`; expose a `/admin/flush-cell/{geohash}` endpoint so operators can force-refresh a cell on demand after known bulk changes.
bottlenecks.detection: Export `loc_replication_lag_seconds` (wall-clock delta between Postgres commit LSN and consumer's applied LSN); alert at >2s sustained for 30s. Cross-check with a canary: periodically insert a test business and measure time-to-appear in the index.

bottlenecks.title: RoaringBitmap union fanout on coarse-precision queries
bottlenecks.trigger: A 20km radius query uses precision-5 cells (~4.9km) and fetches 9 cells; at precision 5 in a dense urban area each cell's RoaringBitmap can hold 50K+ business_ids, so a single candidates_for_cells call must union 9 × 50K = 450K ids. At 35K peak QPS with even 10% coarse-radius traffic (~3.5K QPS), that's ~1.5B bitmap ops/sec across the fleet.
bottlenecks.symptom: Location Service CPU climbs to 70–90% on bitmap unions while memory bandwidth saturates; p99 latency drifts from the advertised 1–3ms range to 10–20ms, and concurrency (sized at 10K) is increasingly gated by CPU rather than request count; downstream API replicas see elevated serviceTimeMs on the loc call.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap returned candidate sets (e.g. truncate to top-N by a pre-sorted spatial order per cell) and force very-coarse queries to skip the candidate shortcut and go straight to PostGIS ST_DWithin, which handles bulk spatial pruning better than in-memory union; pre-compute and cache union results for the top-1000 hot (cell, precision) combos in-process with a 30s TTL.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram of `loc_candidates_returned` and `loc_union_duration_ms` bucketed by precision; alert when p95 candidates > 10K or p95 union duration > 5ms. Track CPU utilization per replica and correlate with precision-5/4 request share.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a separate Location Service For a Yelp-style "nearby" service, every `/nearby` request has to answer the same question before it can do anything useful: *which geohash cells does this (lat, lng, radius) cover, and which business IDs live in those cells?* That's pure geospatial math plus a big in-memory lookup table — it has nothing to do with HTTP handling, auth, or response shaping. The Location Service isolates that work behind a stable interface so the Proximity API can stay dumb about *how* candidates are found. Today it's geohash; tomorrow it might be Google S2 or a quadtree, and swapping the implementation shouldn't force the API tier to change. ## What happens without it Fold this logic into the Proximity API and two things break. First, every one of the ~15 API replicas has to hold its own copy of the 3.2 GB cell→business_id index and its own replication consumer — that's 48 GB of duplicated RAM and 15 Postgres replication slots instead of a handful. Second, when you want to experiment with S2 cells or adaptive quadtrees, you're editing the same codebase that handles auth, pagination, and response shaping — risky changes to a hot path serving 35K QPS. ## The arithmetic With 200M businesses averaging ~30 per precision-6 cell, you get ~7M cells. Storing those as RoaringBitmaps of business IDs fits in ~1.5 GB — small enough to keep entirely in-process, so candidate lookups are 1–3ms memory reads instead of 10–40ms PostGIS queries. At 35K peak QPS, that difference is the whole 100ms p99 budget. ## The trade-off One more network hop (~1–2ms) and a service to operate, in exchange for a swappable spatial index and a much smaller memory footprint across the fleet.

geoidx.name: Geohash Index
geoidx.summary: In-memory map of `geohash_cell → [business_id,...]` held inside the Location Service; the first-pass candidate generator.

sections.heading: Data shape
sections.body:
```
cells: Map<string /*geohash*/, RoaringBitmap<business_id>>
# e.g. cells["9q8yy"] = {17, 4821, 9912, 100221,...}
```
Roaring bitmaps give dense sets with fast intersection — critical if we start combining spatial + category filters.

sections.heading: Size
sections.body: 200M businesses, avg cell occupancy ~30 at precision 6 → ~7M cells. Bitmap compression → ~1.5 GB in RAM.

sections.heading: Query
sections.body: `cells[geohash] ∪ cells[n] for n in neighbors(geohash)` returns candidate business_ids. Typically 50–500 candidates per query — small enough to fetch in one Redis mget or PostGIS IN (...).

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Stale (up to 1s): a newly created business may not appear until the next replication-stream tick — acceptable for 'nearby'.
- Process restart: reload takes ~30s from PostGIS snapshot; in the meantime requests bypass Location Service and go straight to PostGIS (slower but correct).

lost: PostGIS bears all 35K QPS — needs much larger fleet
No place to share a 'hot cell' cache

bottlenecks.title: Cold-start reload window leaves queries unindexed for ~30s
bottlenecks.trigger: Process restart (deploy, OOM, node replacement) on a Location Service replica forces a full rebuild of the 7M-cell, 1.5 GB RoaringBitmap index from a PostGIS snapshot. The stated reload time is ~30s; during that window this replica cannot answer candidates_for_cells and the Proximity API must fall back to raw PostGIS ST_DWithin at 35K peak QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 /nearby latency jumps from ~15ms to 100–300ms during rolling deploys; PostGIS concurrency ceiling (300) is breached and connection pool saturates, producing 503s and empty results. Alert noise on ‘pg_connections_in_use’ and bimodal latency histograms.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Snapshot the RoaringBitmap index to S3/local disk every 5 min and mmap on startup (2–5s reload vs 30s); gate /readyz on index_ready=true so the LB doesn’t send traffic until warmed; stagger replica restarts so N-1 are always warm; keep a global fallback to PostGIS rate-limited to protect the DB.
bottlenecks.detection: Expose gauge `geoidx_ready` (0/1) and counter `geoidx_load_seconds` per replica; alert when any replica is not-ready >10s or when the ratio of ready replicas drops below 80%. Track PostGIS fallback QPS as a leading indicator of index unavailability.

bottlenecks.title: Union fan-out on coarse-precision queries blows CPU and memory bandwidth
bottlenecks.trigger: A 20km-radius request maps to precision-5 cells (~4.9km). In dense urban geographies each cell’s RoaringBitmap can hold 50K+ business_ids, so a single 9-cell union returns ~450K candidate ids. With ~10% of 35K peak QPS being coarse-radius (~3.5K QPS), that is ~1.5B bitmap element operations/sec across the fleet.
bottlenecks.symptom: Location Service CPU climbs from ~30% to 70–90% on bitmap unions; p99 service time drifts from the advertised 1–3ms to 10–20ms; the Proximity API sees its `loc` call time budget evaporate and p99 /nearby latency approaches the 100ms SLO. Horizontal scaling shows diminishing returns because queries are memory-bandwidth-bound, not I/O-bound.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap candidate-set size per cell at precision ≤ 5 (e.g., return top-N pre-sorted by spatial ordering) and force coarse-radius queries to bypass the candidate shortcut straight to PostGIS, which prunes better with a GiST scan than an in-memory 450K-id union; pre-compute 30s TTL union results for the hottest ~1000 (cell, precision) pairs; consider S2 cell hierarchy for cheaper covering.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `geoidx_candidates_returned` and `geoidx_union_duration_ms` bucketed by precision; alert when p95 candidates >10K or p95 union duration >5ms. Track CPU% per replica and correlate spikes with precision-4/5 request share.

bottlenecks.title: Replication-lag-driven staleness during bulk business updates
bottlenecks.trigger: Steady-state writes are ~12/sec but admin backfills or map-data refreshes (e.g., 10K business relocations in a batch) can burst the Postgres logical-replication stream far above the single-threaded consumer’s apply rate, pushing the advertised <1s lag to tens of seconds. A relocated business then lives in the old cell’s bitmap and is absent from the new cell’s bitmap.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users near relocated businesses see phantom results (candidate passes but Haversine post-filter drops it) or missing-result complaints for newly added hot spots; operators notice high `replication_lag_seconds` on the Location Service consumer while /nearby results disagree with the PostGIS source of truth.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the replication consumer by hash(business_id) across 8 workers so apply throughput scales; add backpressure to bulk-import tooling when `geoidx_replication_lag_seconds > 5`; expose an admin `/flush-cell/{geohash}` to force-resync affected cells after known bulk operations; use UNLINK for bitmap mutations to avoid blocking.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `geoidx_replication_lag_seconds` (wall-clock delta between Postgres commit LSN and consumer-applied LSN); alert on >2s sustained for 30s. Run a canary: periodically insert/relocate a synthetic business and measure time-to-appear in the index; alert when canary E2E latency >5s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a Geohash Index in a "nearby" service For a proximity service answering "restaurants within 500m of me," the hard question is: *which businesses are even candidates?* PostGIS could answer this with `ST_DWithin` on every request, but at 35K peak QPS that's 35K spatial index scans per second against a 200 GB table — PostGIS tops out around 300 concurrent queries per node, so you'd need dozens of read replicas just to stay afloat. The Geohash Index sidesteps this by pre-bucketing all 200M businesses into ~7M geohash cells held in RAM as Roaring Bitmaps. A "nearby" query becomes "union the bitmaps for 9 cells" — a pure memory operation returning candidate IDs in 1–3ms. ## What breaks without it Remove this index and every cache miss goes straight to PostGIS. When a cold cell gets queried (say, a suburban area not in the hot-1000), the API has to run `ST_DWithin` over a 200 GB table. Under load, PostGIS connection pools saturate, p99 latency blows past the 100ms budget, and users see spinners or empty "no restaurants found" screens. The Redis Cell Cache helps for *hot* cells, but it can't save you from the long tail of cold lookups — that's what the Geohash Index is for. ## The arithmetic 200M businesses ÷ ~7M cells ≈ **30 businesses per cell** at precision 6. A 9-cell neighborhood fetch returns ~270 candidate IDs — small enough to post-filter with exact Haversine in microseconds, versus PostGIS's 10–40ms per spatial scan. The trade-off: ~1.5 GB of RAM per Location Service replica and a 30-second rebuild on restart, in exchange for taking 99% of spatial-lookup load off PostGIS.

cache.name: Redis Cell Cache
cache.summary: Redis cluster caching precomputed nearby-results per (geohash_cell, category) combo.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body: Key `near:{geohash}:{category}` → JSON of top-100 businesses in that cell (id, name, lat, lng, rating, thumbnail). TTL 5 min — cell membership rarely changes faster than that.

sections.heading: Hit-ratio economics
sections.body: The top 1000 geohash cells see ~40% of all queries (landmarks, downtowns). With a 5-min TTL and ~35K QPS, each hot cell receives ~14 QPS hits → 5-min TTL amortizes the expensive PostGIS fill across ~4000 requests. Hit ratio target 85%+.

sections.heading: Eviction
sections.body: `allkeys-lru` with 2 GB memory cap. Working set (1K hot cells * ~50 KB * ~30 categories ≈ 1.5 GB) fits comfortably.

sections.heading: Invalidation
sections.body: On a PATCH /businesses/:id that changes location or category, invalidate `near:{old_cell}:*` and `near:{new_cell}:*` via Redis SCAN + DEL.

gained: Simpler, slightly lower latency on pure GET
lost: No SCAN for invalidation — we'd need an external index of keys per cell
Lower shared hit ratio (each replica warms independently)

bottlenecks.title: Thundering-herd cache stampede on hot-cell TTL expiry
bottlenecks.trigger: A hot cell (e.g. Times Square) receives ~14 QPS per category × ~30 categories ≈ 420 QPS concentrated on keys sharing the same 5-min TTL. When `near:{cell}:restaurant` expires, all in-flight requests within that cell's category miss simultaneously. Across the top-1000 hot cells handling ~40% of 35K peak QPS (~14K QPS), synchronized expirations route hundreds of concurrent identical PostGIS ST_DWithin queries through the ~15 API replicas.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 5-minute p99 latency spikes from ~15ms to 200ms+; PostGIS connection pool saturates (300 concurrency limit breached); elevated 503s from the LB; bimodal latency histograms visible in dashboards at exactly TTL-multiple intervals.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add ±60s TTL jitter on every SETEX so expirations decorrelate across cells and categories; implement single-flight request coalescing at the API layer (per-key in-flight map) so only one PostGIS query fills each (cell, category); adopt stale-while-revalidate — serve stale cached JSON up to 30s past TTL while a background fetch refreshes. Use `SET... EX 300 XX` semantics where possible to avoid racing writers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on PostGIS QPS exceeding 3K (2× the 1.7K steady-state expectation); alert when `api_cache_miss_ratio` spikes >20% for >10s; histogram `cache_fill_duration_ms` per (cell, category) and watch for coordinated spikes at 5-min boundaries.

bottlenecks.title: SCAN-based invalidation blocks Redis single-threaded command loop
bottlenecks.trigger: Every PATCH to a business with a location change fires `SCAN match=near:{cell}:*` across 9 affected cells × ~30 categories, plus the SCAN itself is O(N) over the ~30K-key keyspace. Steady state at 12 writes/sec is fine, but bulk admin imports or map-data refreshes (e.g. 10K relocations after a vendor data sync) can burst to thousands of SCANs/sec — each SCAN blocks Redis's single command execution thread while 35K QPS of MGETs queue behind it.
bottlenecks.symptom: During bulk writes, /nearby latency from the same Redis cluster climbs from 1–3ms to 50–100ms; Redis CPU pinned at 100%; cache hit ratio drops as SET backfills contend with SCANs; on-call sees `redis_commandstats_scan_usec_per_call` climbing and `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` paradoxically falling under write load.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a reverse index `cell_keys:{cell}` as a Redis SET containing live category keys per cell; invalidation becomes `SMEMBERS cell_keys:{cell}` + `UNLINK` of ~30 keys — O(categories) instead of O(keyspace). Use `UNLINK` (non-blocking) instead of `DEL` for multi-key deletes. Rate-limit bulk-invalidation via a queue bounded at ~100 invalidations/sec.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis `SCAN` command rate >10/sec sustained; alert on `commandstats` p99 latency >5ms; track PATCH-driven invalidation fan-out — alert when >500 key deletions/sec; monitor `cache_key_count` per cell to catch keyspace bloat from missed invalidations.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key concentration overloads a single Redis shard
bottlenecks.trigger: Top 1000 geohash cells handle ~40% of all queries (~14K QPS at peak). In a sharded Redis cluster, `near:{cell}:{category}` keys for a single landmark (e.g. Times Square at precision 7) all hash to one shard — ~30 category variants × ~14 QPS each = ~420 QPS per landmark concentrated on a single node, and a handful of megacities can push a single shard past 5K QPS while others sit idle. MGETs spanning 9 neighbor cells also cross shards, requiring client-side fan-out.
bottlenecks.symptom: Uneven Redis shard CPU (one shard at 80%, others at 20%); p99 MGET latency tail driven entirely by the hottest shard; scaling the cluster horizontally does not reduce peak shard load because the hot key distribution is inherent to geography; cross-slot MGET errors if using Redis Cluster without hash tags.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a small in-process L1 LRU (~50MB) per API replica for the top ~100 cells with 10–30s TTL — absorbs ~60% of hot-cell reads before they hit Redis; use hash tags `near:{9q8zn8u}:restaurant` so all categories of one cell land on the same shard (enables pipelined MGET) while still distributing landmarks across shards; run read replicas per shard for hot-shard reads.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` and CPU dashboards; alert when max-shard QPS / avg-shard QPS ratio >3×; track top-N key access via `redis-cli --hotkeys` sampling; alert on p99 shard latency >5ms when cluster-average is <2ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis sits between the API and PostGIS For a Yelp-style "nearby" service, the expensive part of every query is the PostGIS `ST_DWithin` call — a spatial index scan over a 200 GB table that takes 10–40ms and can only run a few hundred concurrently per database node. But here's the key observation: **most queries aren't unique.** Times Square, downtown SF, the Las Vegas Strip — a small number of geohash cells get hammered by millions of tourists asking the same "restaurants near me" question. Redis turns that repetition into free throughput: compute the answer for `near:9q8zn8u:restaurant` once, cache it for 5 minutes, serve the next 4,000 requests for that cell from RAM in 1–3ms. ## What breaks without it Rip Redis out and every `/nearby` call falls through to PostGIS. At 35K peak QPS against a database that handles ~300 concurrent queries per node, the connection pool saturates in seconds. Users see spinners and empty "no restaurants found" screens during lunch rush; on-call sees `pg_connections_in_use` pinned at 100% and replica lag climbing as read traffic overwhelms the primary. You'd need to 10× the Postgres fleet to compensate — expensive and operationally painful. ## The arithmetic The top 1,000 geohash cells absorb ~40% of all traffic. At 35K peak QPS, that's ~14K QPS flowing through a ~2 GB Redis working set. With an 85% hit ratio target, only **35K × 0.15 ≈ 5.2K QPS** reaches PostGIS — well inside its ~1.7K steady-state comfort zone with headroom for bursts. ## The trade-off Cached results can be up to 5 minutes stale, and invalidation on business edits becomes a fan-out problem — acceptable because "nearby" users don't notice if a restaurant's hours updated 90 seconds ago.

pg.name: Businesses DB (Postgres + PostGIS)
pg.summary: Authoritative Postgres store with PostGIS extension; GiST spatial index on the geography column for exact radius filtering.

sections.heading: Schema
Query
sections.body:
```
SELECT id, name, category, rating, ST_Y(location::geometry) AS lat, ST_X(location::geometry) AS lng, ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint($lng, $lat)::geography) AS dist_m
FROM businesses
WHERE ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint($lng, $lat)::geography, $radius_m) AND category = $cat
ORDER BY dist_m ASC
LIMIT $limit;
```
The GiST index prunes >99% of rows before the distance calc.

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: At 200 GB we can stay single-primary with read replicas. If growth pushes multi-TB, shard by continent/country (CA, US-West, US-East, EU, …) because nearby queries are intrinsically local — cross-shard scatter is rare.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: Single-primary strong consistency for writes; reads served from replicas with <100ms lag. Because 'nearby' tolerates seconds of staleness, replica reads are fine.

gained: Combined text + geo query natively (search 'pizza near me')
lost: Less precise distance than PostGIS spheroid math
No exact radius filter in DB — candidate set post-filtered in app

bottlenecks.title: Connection pool saturation on cold-cell miss storms
bottlenecks.trigger: PostGIS handles only ~300 concurrent queries per node, and steady-state traffic hitting PG should be ~1.7K QPS (15% miss of 35K peak). A correlated Redis TTL expiry across hot cells or a Redis partial outage pushes effective miss-rate from 15% toward 50%+, sending 15K+ QPS at the ~300-slot pool. Each ST_DWithin takes 10–40ms, so 300 slots × ~50 QPS/slot ≈ 15K QPS ceiling — anything beyond queues or errors.
bottlenecks.symptom: pg_stat_activity shows 300 active connections pinned; new API requests block on pool checkout for 100ms–several seconds; /nearby p99 blows past the 100ms SLO; LB reports surge of 503s and connection timeouts; PostGIS CPU climbs to 90%+ while buffer cache thrashes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of Postgres to multiplex the ~750 API-side connections (15 replicas × 50) onto ~200 backend connections; size statement_timeout=150ms so stuck queries don't hog slots; add 2–4 read replicas behind a HAProxy and route /nearby to replicas (writes-only to primary); implement circuit breaker in API that sheds load to 'degraded mode' returning stale Redis data when pg_pool_wait_ms p95 > 50ms.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pg_stat_activity.count > 240 (80% of 300) sustained for 30s; alert on pg_pool_wait_time_ms p95 > 20ms; alert on pg_stat_statements mean_exec_time for ST_DWithin > 40ms; track connections-per-API-replica histogram to detect uneven distribution.

bottlenecks.title: GiST index bloat and VACUUM contention at 200GB scale
bottlenecks.trigger: 200M rows × 1KB = 200GB + ~50GB GiST index. At 1M updates/day (12/sec steady, burst to 100s/sec during admin imports), HOT-update eligibility is low because geography column changes touch the GiST index; dead tuples accumulate. Autovacuum on a 250GB table can take hours and compete with the 1.7K QPS read workload for I/O bandwidth.
bottlenecks.symptom: Query planner starts preferring seq scans over GiST as statistics go stale; ST_DWithin latency drifts from 10–40ms baseline to 80–200ms; bloated GiST index inflates from 50GB toward 100GB+ on disk; autovacuum_workers saturated and 'autovacuum: VACUUM businesses' runs for hours visible in pg_stat_progress_vacuum; replica lag spikes during vacuum due to WAL volume.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.02 (from default 0.2) and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit=2000 for this table specifically; schedule weekly REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on idx_biz_location during off-peak; partition businesses by continent/country (matching the sharding plan) so vacuum operates on 20–50GB partitions instead of 250GB monolith; enable pg_repack for online bloat removal.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup / n_live_tup > 0.2 for businesses table; monitor pg_relation_size('idx_biz_location') growth rate — alert on >10% week-over-week; track pg_stat_progress_vacuum duration and alert when vacuum runs > 2h.

bottlenecks.title: Replication lag to read replicas during bulk imports
bottlenecks.trigger: Steady-state writes are 12/sec and replication lag stays <100ms, but bulk admin imports (e.g., 10K business relocations from a vendor data refresh) generate ~10K UPDATEs that each touch the GiST index. Logical replication is single-threaded apply per subscription; physical streaming replication can fall seconds-to-minutes behind while the replica replays WAL with GiST index maintenance.
bottlenecks.symptom: Location Service's logical-replication consumer reports lag growing from <1s to 30s+; /nearby queries served from replicas return stale candidate sets (newly relocated businesses still in old cells); cache backfills from PG write stale data into Redis for 5min TTL; on-call sees pg_stat_replication.replay_lag climbing; user complaints about 'phantom' results that fail the Haversine post-filter.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Rate-limit bulk-import tooling to 50 writes/sec using an application-level token bucket; set max_wal_senders=10 and wal_compression=on to reduce replica catch-up I/O; for logical replication into Location Service, shard the subscription by hash(business_id) across 8 parallel workers; add backpressure: pause bulk imports when pg_stat_replication.replay_lag > 5s.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pg_stat_replication.replay_lag > 2s sustained for 30s; alert on pg_wal_receiver lag bytes > 100MB; canary test: insert synthetic business every minute and measure time-to-visibility on replica, alert when >5s; dashboard correlation between bulk-import QPS and replica lag.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why PostGIS is the authoritative store here For a Yelp-style proximity service, *someone* has to be the source of truth about the 200M businesses in the world — their exact coordinates, hours, categories, owner, rating. Redis is a cache (data can vanish), and the in-memory Geohash Index only holds business IDs, not the rich fields the app needs to render. PostGIS is where the durable, queryable, exact data lives. The "PostGIS" part matters specifically because a 500m radius search isn't just "find rows in a box" — it needs true spheroid distance math (`ST_DWithin`) so a restaurant at 499m is included and one at 501m isn't. A plain B-tree index can't do that; the GiST spatial index can. ## What breaks without it Rip PostGIS out and you have no system of record. Redis evictions would permanently lose businesses. Worse, the geohash-cell approach always returns candidates from *rectangular* cells — without `ST_DWithin` as the final filter, users on the edge of a cell would see restaurants that are actually 1.5km away when they asked for 500m. The app feels broken ("why is this so far?"), and owners have nowhere to reliably update their hours. ## The arithmetic 200M businesses × ~1 KB/row = **200 GB of data + ~50 GB for the GiST index**, fitting comfortably on one primary with read replicas. With Redis absorbing 85% of the 35K peak QPS, only ~5K QPS hits PostGIS — well within the ~300-concurrent-query ceiling per node when paired with PgBouncer. ## Trade-off Single-primary Postgres caps write throughput, but at 12 writes/sec steady-state that headroom is enormous — the designer traded horizontal write scaling for exact spatial correctness.

userloc.name: User-Location Service
userloc.summary: Tracks the last-reported location of each user (for 'deliver near me' style features and personalization); kept in Redis with short TTL.

sections.heading: Why separate
sections.body: User location is high-write, short-lived, and orthogonal to business data. Mixing it into PostGIS would balloon write QPS and trash the GiST index with constant updates.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Redis key `user_loc:{user_id}` → `{lat, lng, accuracy, ts}`, TTL 10 min. Updated on each /nearby call (piggyback) or on explicit POST /me/location.

sections.heading: Use cases in proximity service
sections.body:
- Personalize 'nearby' by comparing the current request's lat/lng against recent history — cross-city teleport may indicate a bug or a new trip (bias results differently)
- Feed 'friends nearby' features in a companion service

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.body: Location is PII — Redis is TLS-in-transit and encrypted-at-rest; user can delete with DELETE /me/location which DELs the key.

gained: Durable log for offline analytics (heatmaps, trip replays)
lost: No direct point-lookup — need a consumer materializing into Redis anyway

bottlenecks.title: Write QPS from piggybacked /nearby updates saturates Redis
bottlenecks.trigger: Every /nearby call piggybacks a SETEX on user_loc:{user_id}. At 35K peak QPS of nearby searches, that's 35K writes/sec against the User-Location Redis — on top of any explicit POST /me/location traffic. A single Redis node tops out around 80–100K ops/sec mixed workload, but with TLS-in-transit and encrypted-at-rest overhead, effective throughput can drop to 30–50K ops/sec, putting the service at or near its ceiling during peak.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis CPU pinned near 100% on the primary; SETEX latency climbs from 1–3ms advertised to 10–30ms; /nearby p99 tail grows because even fire-and-forget writes back-pressure the API event loop when the connection pool saturates; on-call sees redis_instantaneous_ops_per_sec plateaued while client-side command queue depth grows.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard Redis by hash(user_id) across 4–8 nodes so write QPS divides linearly; batch location updates client-side (only SETEX if last update >60s old or user moved >50m) to cut write volume by ~5–10×; make the piggyback write truly async via a bounded in-process queue with drop-on-overflow so it never back-pressures the /nearby response path; consider a write-behind pattern where API appends to a local ring buffer flushed every 500ms in one pipelined MSET.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_instantaneous_ops_per_sec > 40K per node sustained 30s; alert on SETEX command p99 > 5ms; track ratio of user_loc writes to /nearby QPS (should stay <1.0 with batching); monitor API-side fire-and-forget queue depth and dropped-write counter.

bottlenecks.title: Memory footprint grows unbounded during DAU spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: 500M DAU × ~100 bytes per user_loc entry (JSON: lat, lng, accuracy, ts, plus Redis key overhead ~80B) ≈ 90 GB of working-set memory if every daily active user has a live TTL entry. During global peak hours (e.g., Asia evening + EU afternoon overlap), concurrent live keys can spike to 150M+ users × 100B ≈ 15 GB on a single unsharded Redis instance — well past the typical 8–16GB per-node sweet spot where RDB snapshot forks and AOF rewrites start causing latency hiccups.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis memory usage climbs steadily through the day; BGSAVE forks take 10+ seconds and stall command processing during the copy-on-write page-fault storm; evictions start on maxmemory pressure, kicking out recent user locations prematurely (before the 10min TTL); replication lag spikes during RDB snapshot hand-off to replicas.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard across N Redis nodes so each holds <10GB working set; use Redis Hash encoding with hash-max-ziplist-entries tuning to pack multiple users per key (e.g., user_loc:{shard}:{bucket} as a hash of 100 users) cutting per-entry overhead by ~3×; shorten TTL from 10min to 5min for inactive users; disable RDB and use AOF with everysec for durability without fork stalls; cap maxmemory with allkeys-lru policy as a safety valve.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis used_memory > 70% of maxmemory; alert on BGSAVE/AOF-rewrite duration > 2s; track evicted_keys counter — should be near zero; dashboard used_memory and connected_clients correlated with DAU curve.

bottlenecks.title: PII deletion latency and GDPR compliance gap
bottlenecks.trigger: DELETE /me/location does a single Redis DEL on user_loc:{user_id} — but Redis replication is async, and the key may still exist on read replicas for tens of ms to seconds. Worse, if AOF is enabled and a backup/snapshot captured the key, the deleted location persists in backup artifacts indefinitely, violating the 'user can delete' privacy guarantee. Additionally, with sharded Redis, a DELETE must hit the correct shard; a stale routing config or failover during deletion can leave orphaned keys.
bottlenecks.symptom: Audit/compliance team flags user-reported deletions where location data reappears in analytics dumps; legal escalation for GDPR 'right to erasure' requests when restored-from-backup Redis contains deleted user_loc entries; user support tickets reporting that 'friends nearby' still shows them after deletion.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a deletion tombstone set (deleted_users:{user_id} with 30-day TTL) that the read path checks before returning a user_loc entry, so even a restored-from-backup key is masked; use Redis UNLINK instead of DEL for non-blocking deletion; propagate deletions to downstream 'friends nearby' consumers via a dedicated deletion topic; exclude user_loc:* from long-term backups (snapshot-on-replica with short retention only); document that TTL 10min means uncontested erasure completes within 10min maximum even without explicit DELETE.
bottlenecks.detection: Canary test: issue DELETE /me/location for a synthetic user and verify key absence on all replicas within 1s; alert if delete-to-gone latency p99 > 2s; audit log every DELETE /me/location with shard and replica confirmation; scan backup artifacts monthly for deleted-user keys as a compliance check.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a separate User-Location Service for a Yelp-style proximity app The **Businesses DB** (PostGIS) holds 200M rows that change ~12 times per second — new restaurants, edited hours. That's a read-heavy, write-rare table, which is exactly why a GiST spatial index on it works so well. But *user* location is the opposite: every `/nearby` call produces a fresh (lat, lng) ping for the calling user, and at 35K peak QPS that's 35K writes per second of transient data. If you stuffed those into PostGIS alongside businesses, you'd be issuing 35K UPDATEs/sec against a table optimized for reads — the GiST index would thrash, autovacuum would fall behind, and your 100ms p99 budget for `/nearby` would evaporate. So the design isolates user pings into Redis with a 10-minute TTL: the data is short-lived, the access pattern is point-lookup by `user_id`, and it never needs to survive a restart. ## What breaks without it Merge user locations into PostGIS and the very first lunch rush pins write QPS at ~35K against a database that handles ~12 writes/sec comfortably. Operators see replica lag climb into minutes, `/nearby` latency doubles as GiST index pages get dirtied constantly, and features like "friends nearby" have no fast way to answer "where was user 12 five minutes ago?" without a full table scan. ## The arithmetic 35K peak `/nearby` QPS × 1 piggybacked location write each = **35K writes/sec**. Redis handles that on one shard (~80K ops/sec ceiling); PostGIS would need a 1000× write-capacity expansion. The trade-off: user locations are now non-durable — a Redis failure loses the last 10 minutes of pings, which is fine because the next `/nearby` call rewrites them anyway.

operations.title: Search nearby (cached cell HIT)
operations.name: Search nearby (cached cell HIT)
operations.description: User taps 'nearby restaurants' near Union Square, SF. The cell is hot in Redis; API returns in ~8ms p50.

steps.title: App asks for restaurants within 500 m
steps.action: Mobile app reads OS location, then issues GET /nearby with lat/lng, radius, and category.
steps.codeOrCommand:
const pos = await navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition;
fetch(`/nearby?lat=${pos.coords.latitude}&lng=${pos.coords.longitude}` + `&radius=500&category=restaurant&limit=20`);

steps.title: LB routes to an API replica
steps.action: Round-robin pick, least-connections tiebreak.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick("round_robin", healthy_only=True)
forward(req -> upstream)

steps.title: API validates and picks geohash precision
steps.action: Clamp radius to [10 m, 50 km]. For 500m radius, select precision 7 (≈150 m cells). Compute the center cell and its 8 neighbors.
steps.codeOrCommand:
radius = min(max(req.radius, 10), 50_000)
prec = precision_for(radius) # 500m → 7
center = geohash.encode(req.lat, req.lng, prec)
# center = '9q8zn8u'
cells = [center] + geohash.neighbors(center)
# cells = ['9q8zn8u','9q8zn8v','9q8zn8s','9q8zn8t',
# '9q8zn8w','9q8zn8g','9q8zn8e','9q8zn8d','9q8zn89']

steps.title: Location Service confirms cell layout
steps.action: Canonicalizes the cell list (sorted, deduped) so Redis keys are stable. Returns the same 9 cells back to the API along with the cache key template.
steps.codeOrCommand: def candidates_for_cells(cells, category): cells = sorted(set(cells)) return [(c, f"near:{c}:{category}") for c in cells]

steps.title: API pipelined MGET on 9 Redis keys
steps.action: Single round-trip MGET for all 9 cells. Union of their business lists forms the candidate set.
steps.codeOrCommand:
MGET near:9q8zn8u:restaurant near:9q8zn8v:restaurant...
# 9 values returned, all non-nil (hot downtown cells)
steps.decision: All 9 cells HIT → skip PostGIS entirely

steps.title: API updates user's last-known location (parallel)
steps.action: Fire-and-forget SET on Redis so downstream personalization features have fresh context. Does not block the response.
steps.codeOrCommand:
redis.setex( f"user_loc:{user.id}", 600, json.dumps({"lat": 37.7879, "lng": -122.4075, "ts": now_epoch})
)

steps.title: API post-filters by exact distance and ranks
steps.action: The candidate set includes some businesses beyond 500 m (corner-of-cell artifacts). Exact Haversine distance is cheap at 184 rows. Sort by distance and take top 20.
steps.codeOrCommand:
filtered = [ b for b in candidates if haversine_m(req.lat, req.lng, b.lat, b.lng) <= req.radius
]
filtered.sort(key=lambda b: haversine_m(req.lat, req.lng, b.lat, b.lng))
results = filtered[:20]

steps.title: API builds 200 response
steps.action: Shape the payload with id, name, rating, distance, and a cursor for pagination.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response( status=200, headers={"Cache-Control": "private, max-age=30"}, body={ "results": [ {"id": b.id, "name": b.name, "distance_m": round(b.dist, 1), "rating": b.rating, "lat": b.lat, "lng": b.lng} for b in results ], "cursor": "eyJvZmY...", "source": "cache" }
)

steps.title: LB relays the response
steps.action: Return path — no routing decision.

steps.title: App renders 20 pins on the map
steps.action: Total wall-clock ~30–80ms depending on mobile network. All on the hot path; PostGIS never touched for this user.
steps.codeOrCommand:
for (const biz of resp.results) { map.addMarker({lat: biz.lat, lng: biz.lng, title: biz.name});
}

operations.title: Search nearby (cached cell MISS → PostGIS)
operations.name: Search nearby (cached cell MISS → PostGIS)
operations.description: User in a less-trafficked suburban area. The cell is cold; API falls through to PostGIS, backfills Redis, and returns. ~40ms p50.

steps.title: User searches nearby from a quiet area
steps.action: Same request shape, different geography.
steps.codeOrCommand: fetch(`/nearby?lat=44.9537&lng=-93.0900&radius=2000&category=cafe&limit=20`);

steps.title: LB forwards to API
steps.action: Standard routing.

steps.title: API picks precision 6 (2km radius)
steps.action: 2km → precision 6 cells (~1.2 km). Compute center + 8 neighbors.
steps.codeOrCommand:
prec = precision_for(2000) # 6
center = geohash.encode(44.9537, -93.0900, prec) # 'dp8nc'
cells = [center] + geohash.neighbors(center)

steps.title: Location Service canonicalizes cells
steps.action: Same helper as the hot path.
steps.codeOrCommand: return [(c, f"near:{c}:cafe") for c in sorted(cells)]

steps.title: Redis returns mostly nils (MISS)
steps.action: 7 of 9 keys are absent — these cells haven't been queried in at least 5 min.
steps.codeOrCommand:
MGET near:dp8nc:cafe near:dp8nd:cafe...
# results: [null, null, [6 businesses], null, null, null, [3 businesses], null, null]
steps.decision: 7/9 cells MISS → fall through to PostGIS for the missing ones

steps.title: Location Service checks its in-memory candidate index
steps.action: Rather than hitting PostGIS blind, the Proximity API asks the geohash index for candidate business_ids in the missing cells. This often narrows the PostGIS query from a radius-scan to an ID-IN lookup.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# in-process
biz_ids = for c in missing_cells: biz_ids.extend(index.cells[c]) # RoaringBitmap union
# → e.g. 47 business ids

steps.title: API runs ST_DWithin on PostGIS for the missing cells
steps.action: Use the candidate id list as an additional predicate so the GiST index scan stays tight. Category filter applied in-query.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT id, name, category, rating, ST_Y(location::geometry) AS lat, ST_X(location::geometry) AS lng, ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint(-93.0900, 44.9537)::geography) AS dist_m
FROM businesses
WHERE id = ANY($1) -- candidate shortcut AND category = 'cafe' AND ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint(-93.0900, 44.9537)::geography, 2000)
ORDER BY dist_m ASC;

steps.title: API backfills the missing cell keys (parallel)
steps.action: Write SET for each of the 7 missing cells with the per-cell subset. TTL 5 min. Fire-and-forget — doesn't block the user response.

steps.title: API merges cache hits + PostGIS rows, filters, returns
steps.action: Same post-filter + sort as the hot path. Response labels source='mixed'.
steps.codeOrCommand:
all_rows = cache_hits + pg_rows
filtered = [b for b in all_rows if haversine_m(req.lat, req.lng, b.lat, b.lng) <= req.radius]
filtered.sort(key=lambda b: b.dist_m)
return Response(body={"results": filtered[:20], "source": "mixed"})

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: App renders pins
steps.action: Wall-clock ~60–120ms (cold cell plus PostGIS round-trip). Next user in the same cell within 5 min will hit cache.
steps.note: If 9 PostGIS queries (one per cell) were issued naively the latency would balloon — the app batches them into one ST_DWithin over the whole 9-cell neighborhood.

operations.title: Update a business listing
operations.name: Update a business listing
operations.description: Owner edits the cafe's hours. API writes PostGIS, invalidates hot cells in Redis, and the change ripples through replicas within seconds.

steps.title: Owner saves updated hours
steps.action: Business owner web dashboard submits PATCH /businesses/:id.

steps.title: LB forwards PATCH to an API replica
steps.action: Standard routing.

steps.title: API authenticates and validates
steps.action: Verify the owner's token and that they own business 45123.
steps.codeOrCommand:
owner = auth.verify(req.bearer)
biz = db.fetchone("SELECT owner_id, geohash FROM businesses WHERE id = 45123")
if biz is None: return 404
if biz.owner_id!= owner.id: return 403

steps.title: PostGIS updates the business row
steps.action: Simple UPDATE — hours changes do not affect location/geohash, so spatial indexes are untouched.

steps.title: API invalidates hot cells that contain this business (parallel)
steps.action: The business's geohash tells us which cells' cached lists may hold its data (including neighbor cells, for safety). DEL all matching keys across categories.
steps.codeOrCommand:
affected_cells = [biz.geohash] + geohash.neighbors(biz.geohash)
for c in affected_cells: # invalidate all category variants in one SCAN+DEL pass for key in redis.scan_iter(match=f"near:{c}:*", count=100): redis.delete(key)

steps.title: Location Service picks up the change via logical replication (parallel)
steps.action: A background consumer tailing Postgres logical replication notices the UPDATE on business 45123. Because hours changed but location didn't, the in-memory `geoidx` cell map is NOT modified. If location had changed, the old-cell bitmap would lose the id and the new-cell bitmap would gain it.
steps.codeOrCommand: def on_replication_event(ev): if ev.table!= "businesses": return if ev.op == "UPDATE" and "location" in ev.changed_fields: old_cell = ev.before.geohash new_cell = ev.after.geohash index.cells[old_cell].remove(ev.id) index.cells[new_cell].add(ev.id) # hours-only updates do not affect the cell index

steps.title: API returns 200 to the owner
steps.action: Commit succeeded; Redis will refill lazily on next nearby query from this area.

steps.title: LB relays 200
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Dashboard shows 'Saved'
steps.action: Owner sees confirmation. The next 'nearby' query hitting this cell will miss Redis, rebuild the cell cache from PostGIS (now including the new hours), and serve the updated data to users within seconds.
steps.note: Because we use cache invalidation (not write-through) on update, the first post-update nearby query pays a cache-miss penalty. This is an acceptable trade — it keeps the write path simple and avoids cross-category fan-out writes.

tradeoffs.chosen: Geohash cells over quadtree or R-tree
tradeoffs.rationale: Geohashes are opaque strings that slot directly into Redis keys and Postgres B-tree indexes, whereas quadtrees need a bespoke in-memory structure and R-trees lock you into PostGIS. Geohash precision trimming also maps naturally onto the radius-to-cell-size decision.

tradeoffs.chosen: Cache per geohash-6 cell, not per (lat,lng) query
tradeoffs.rationale: Per-query caching has near-zero hit ratio because user coordinates are unique. Per-cell caching lets thousands of nearby users share the same Redis entry for Times Square, pushing the hit ratio north of 85 percent.

tradeoffs.chosen: 60 second eventual consistency for listing edits
tradeoffs.rationale: Strict consistency would force cache-through writes and kill read throughput. Sixty seconds is well below the user's perception of freshness for a business listing and lets the invalidator batch evictions.

Dual-writing to Redis from the API layer risks drift on partial failure. A single writer (PostGIS) plus a Kafka consumer that evicts cells guarantees the cache never lies for longer than the invalidation lag.

tradeoffs.chosen: Shard PostGIS by geohash prefix, not by business_id
tradeoffs.rationale: Most queries are spatial, so colocating rows with neighbouring cells keeps each query on one shard. Hashing by business_id would scatter every radius query across every shard.
